transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2027-01-19 09:32 UTC, Duration 52 mins
Attendees: Maya Lee (Redwood AE), Jonas Kramer (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Nair (Cobalt ML Lead), Sam Ortiz (Cobalt Infra), Liu Wei (Cobalt SRE)
Recording note: phone audio + Zoom screen share, captions on (auto).

Summary: quick deep dive on recent accuracy regressions after AWQ/GPTQ conversions on customer's finetuned medical summarization model, discussion of KV cache entropy effects and batching interactions, and options for on-prem/VPC fallback paths. Agreed to run a mixed-precision KV-warmup benchmark and exchange prompt set.

Topics: quant tradeoffs (INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ), KV cache staleness and 'entropy', prefix caching and sticky sessions, batching vs latency SLOs, on-prem deployment constraints and secure pilot plan.

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Maya Lee: ok good morning, thanks everyone for joining, um today we wanted to run through the regression patterns you saw after applying AWQ and then the g-p-t-q pipeline, and then outline a couple of deploy options we can run to reproduce and mitigate it.
[00:18] Priya Nair: yeah thanks, Maya. we pushed a couple of quant variants last week to a canary and started seeing a subtle drop on clinical summarization precision — like a 3 to 4 percent on entity recall, which is... a bit worrying.
[00:32] Jonas Kramer: thanks Priya, can you remind us which quant flow you used? AWQ first then GPTQ, or a single pass? some folks do AWQ->gptq hybrid and others do a single gptq pass.
[00:46] Priya: we tried AWQ 4-bit per-tensor first, then a gpt q layerwise refit for a few layers, so hybrid. the toolchain was ModelForge's AWQ patch + our internal calibrator.
[01:05] Sam Ortiz: just to add, this was deployed on your dedicated cluster image in our VPC, running 4xA100 40G with the Redwood Dedicated agent. network was normal, no obvious CPU steal.
[01:18] Liu Wei: also noted some KV cache flushes during traffic spikes, not sure if that lines up with the regressions.
[01:27] Jonas: ok that's a useful data point. from our experience, AWQ/GPTQ hybrids sometimes interact poorly with KV cache behavior, especially when you have long prefix reuse — the quantized kernels may introduce tiny output distribution shifts that cascade during autoregression and then KV lookup becomes higher entropy, resulting in a different attention pattern.
[01:50] Priya: can you unpack "higher entropy" there? I'm trying to map that to our eval metrics.
[01:55] Jonas: yah, sure. what I mean is the cache keys/attn weights are slightly perturbed so the hashed indices for identical prefixes diverge, so hit-rate on prefix cache drops, which increases forward compute and changes tokenization alignment sometimes. this is more pronounced for per-channel quantization vs per-tensor — the latter tends to preserve global distribution better but costs memory.
[02:20] Priya: interesting. we do per-channel int8 on some layers and switched to AWQ for the heavy MLPs.
[02:28] Maya: quick note, sometimes the auto-calibrator will try to be too aggressive on outliers — trimming tails that actually encode rare but important clinical tokens. have you tried preserving tail buckets in the calibrator?
[02:40] Priya: we did run with clip at 99.9 but not 99.995, we can try the higher tail.
[02:47] Jonas: also worth checking layer-wise sensitivity. on similar models we saw layer 6 and 9 were super-sensitive: quant there changes attention rolloff and downstream NER recall. we usually run a layer-sweep where we keep those layers FP16 or FP32 and quantize others.
[03:08] Liu Wei: ok if we do that, what's the latency impact? we need 95th < 220ms for chat workflow.
[03:15] Jonas: mixed precision usually adds ~10-20% latency at p95 compared to full int8, but cost wise it's still far better than FP32. depends on batch size and kernel fusion. We'll run a p95 profile in the benchmark.
[03:30] Priya: batching is tricky because our UI sends lots of short prompts, batching helps throughput but increases p95 — we can't sacrifice user experience.
[03:38] Maya: that's typical, so we need to test both single-request latency and controlled batching. Jonas, can the benchmark emulate sticky sessions and prefix cold/warm cycles?
[03:47] Jonas: yes, our perf harness has a KV-warmup mode where we replay realistic prefix distributions and can simulate cold starts and repeated prefix reuse. we'll add a run that toggles KV cache TTL and a "prefix entropy" parameter to artificially perturb inputs.
[04:05] Sam: about the VPC/onprem constraints — our security team wants KMS-managed keys and no outbound egress to third-party model stores. can Redwood Dedicated run completely inside our VPC with HSM integration?
[04:18] Maya: yes, Dedicated in VPC mode supports customer-managed KMS, and for on-prem we provide an air-gapped package. the one caveat is certain optimized kernels we ship require kernel-level drivers and may need a privileged install; we'll share the ops checklist.
[04:33] Priya: does the op checklist include exact driver versions? we've had issues where cuBLAS or driver mismatch cause tiny numeric differences.
[04:41] Jonas: absolutely — we'll include driver matrix and the exact CUDA/cudnn versions. small numeric deltas from different blas libs absolutely can change quant sensitivity.
[04:51] Liu Wei: on the subject of fallbacks, can Redwood run precision cascade at runtime? like try int8, if delta on subset prompts exceeds threshold, fallback to fp16 for that session?
[05:02] Maya: yes, we have a precision-cascade feature in the runtime — it can be configured per-route: try AWQ/int8, if mismatch score > threshold on a short eval, switch to fp16 for the request or session. it's sticky for the session window.
[05:17] Priya: how do you compute mismatch score? is that token-level logprob delta?
[05:22] Jonas: currently we use a composite: per-token logprob delta on a golden prompt set plus an embedding cosine threshold for semantics. it's lightweight but gives a quick signal.
[05:33] Priya: would that add latency? the extra check?
[05:36] Jonas: negligible — we do a small fast comparator on the first few tokens; if it flags, then we kick the request to a fallback path which has higher latency but better quality.
[05:48] Sam: ok operationally, we need audit logs for any fallback switches (for compliance). is that in the console?
[05:55] Maya: yes, every precision switch is logged with the route, timestamp, and diagnostic snapshot. we'll include that in the SOW.
[06:03] Priya: let's talk about evaluation — our offline eval didn't catch this because our test set had low frequency of clinical entities. we probably under-sampled.
[06:12] Jonas: that's common — quant regressions often show up on rare tokens or long-range dependency tests. recommend you expand the eval suite to include adversarial prompts and distribution shift cases.
[06:24] Priya: we'll do that. we also want to know if the AWQ implementation here is known to be less robust for tokenization boundaries — any known failures?
[06:33] Jonas: AWQ per-tensor vs per-channel tradeoff: per-channel preserves per-row scale which helps tokens with skewed activations, but some AWQ variants do grouped channels that can blur boundaries. our playbook has a section on "token-boundary pathologies" and mitigations like increasing calibration bins and layerwise exceptions.
[06:51] Maya: I'll paste the playbook link after the call — short link: https://redwood.ai/quant-playbook (note: internal shorthand).
[06:59] Priya: thanks. another question: we saw regressions only during periods of high concurrent traffic, could that be due to batching + cache eviction interactions?
[07:08] Jonas: yes, two plausible mechanisms: 1) batching increases effective context length in certain kernels, causing KV offset misalignment after quantization; 2) cache eviction during bursts causes re-computation that surfaces quant errors. We'll simulate both.
[07:23] Liu Wei: how do you simulate eviction? we don't want to accidentally blow up our prod tables.
[07:28] Jonas: our harness does synthetic eviction by filling the cache with pseudo-prefixes to force evictions, recording hit/miss and replicating the timeline. we can run this in your staging cluster.
[07:39] Sam: staging currently mirrors prod infra, ok to run. question on metrics: besides entity recall and logprob delta, what other signals should we monitor for early detection?
[07:48] Jonas: monitor prefix cache hit-rate, token-level perplexity drift, embedding drift (cosine sim), and sudden increase in repeated top-token anomalies. We can provide a dashboard template.
[08:02] Priya: is there a recommended canary strategy? we currently do 5% traffic.
[08:07] Maya: for quantization changes, we recommend a sticky canary with route-level A/B and a set of golden prompts that run in shadow mode on 100% traffic but only evaluate offline; then if drift < threshold for 48 hours and no p95 regression, expand to 25% and so on.
[08:25] Priya: shadow mode sounds good, can Redwood do shadow evaluations in VPC?
[08:31] Jonas: yes, shadow evals can be run entirely in-VPC with no egress; they only write logs to your S3-compatible bucket if you permit.
[08:41] Liu Wei: about kernel variants: you mentioned an optimized kernel that uses stochastic rounding, does that change determinism for reproducibility?
[08:50] Jonas: stochastic rounding does introduce non-determinism; for auditable workloads we keep an option for deterministic rounding at some perf cost. we'll note that in the ops checklist.
[08:59] Priya: great. for the on-prem package — if we do air-gapped install, what's the support window?
[09:05] Maya: we provide 90-day enterprise support SLA for on-prem initial installs and extended support as part of the dedicated contract. We also ship a monitoring agent that can push metrics to your internal grafana.
[09:16] Sam: perfect. one more technical: the calibrator we used did per-layer histogram clipping — could histogram bin size cause calibration artifacts?
[09:25] Jonas: yes, very much so. coarse bins can smear out spikes. use adaptive binning for heavy-tailed layers. in our internal tests increasing bins from 256 to 4096 for a few sensitive layers reduced the regression.
[09:40] Priya: that explains why 99.9 clipping didn't help as much — we probably had coarse bins.
[09:46] Maya: ok let's recap the diagnostic plan: Jonas runs three benchmark variants in staging — (A) replicate hybrid AWQ/GPTQ with current calibrator, (B) same but with layer 6/9 FP16 (layer-sweep), (C) mixed-precision with KV-warmup + eviction stress. He'll collect p95, throughput, prefix hit-rate, token logprob delta, and embedding drift.
[10:06] Jonas: yes, and we'll attach raw model activations for the flagged prompts (sanitized) so you can inspect. We'll anonymize logs.
[10:15] Priya: good. I'll prepare prompt set and also pick 30 high-priority clinical cases to audit.
[10:22] Liu Wei: and I'll coordinate staging creds and ensure the test runs in the VPC with required KMS permissions.
[10:29] Maya: final notes: we'll send SOW and SOC2 summary and the quant playbook. Also—one operational tip—if you need immediate mitigation we can enable per-route fallback to fp16 for sessions where the mismatch score exceeds 0.12.
[10:44] Priya: thanks, that might be a good interim.
[10:47] Maya: cool. any other questions?
[10:50] Sam: none from infra.
[10:52] Priya: no, that's it. thanks everyone.

--- End of meeting ---
